note: Non expert persuasion techniques beat algorithmic attacks at over 92 percent success, which widens the realistic threat population.
title: How Johnny Can Persuade LLMs to Jailbreak Them: Rethinking Persuasion to Challenge AI Safety by Humanizing LLMs

reading.body:
Persuasion techniques from everyday conversation can jailbreak leading LLMs over 92 percent of the time, a success rate that exceeds technical attacks and requires no specialized knowledge.

The gap between existing defenses and actual vulnerabilities appears systematic rather than marginal. Current safety measures are built to stop algorithmic attacks. They assume threats come from people with technical expertise who write prompts in ways machines can recognize and block. Persuasion-based attacks work differently. They use social influence principles that mirror how humans naturally communicate, making them harder to distinguish from legitimate use and easier for anyone to execute during routine interaction.

This matters directly for AI scaling because it reframes the binding constraint on safe deployment. Compute unlocks capability, but capability without trustworthy behavior creates liability rather than value. If safety depends on defending against social influence rather than just algorithmic manipulation, the problem space expands beyond what technical architecture alone can solve. Organizations cannot simply add filters. They must address how persuasion techniques can compromise system behavior across categories of harm.

The data covers success rates and attack effectiveness. It does not measure how defenses might improve, whether organizations are actually implementing guards against these methods, or how scaled systems respond differently than the models tested. It shows the vulnerability is real. It does not show whether the vulnerability is fixable through retraining, alignment, or requires different approaches entirely.

explain_beginner: Most well known ways of tricking an AI chatbot into breaking its safety rules involve technical tricks, carefully optimized nonsense text strings or algorithmic search procedures that an average person could not produce by hand. This paper asks a different and arguably more worrying question, can ordinary, everyday persuasion, the kind of rhetorical techniques a salesperson or a persistent friend might use in normal conversation, work just as well? Zeng and coauthors built a systematic taxonomy of persuasion techniques drawn from social science research, things like appealing to authority, framing a request as a small foot in the door ask, or invoking reciprocity, and used it to automatically generate conversational, human sounding prompts designed to talk a model into providing harmful information. Testing this approach against Llama-2, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4, they found it succeeded more than 92 percent of the time, outperforming several purely algorithmic jailbreak methods that came before it. This matters because it means AI safety is not just a technical arms race against clever exploit code, it also has to hold up against completely ordinary conversational persuasion that any user could type without any special skill.
explain_business: The risk this paper surfaces for any business deploying a customer facing or internal conversational AI system is that the attacker population capable of breaking its safety guardrails is much larger than previously assumed, because a greater than 92 percent success rate using ordinary persuasion language means no coding skill, specialized tools, or algorithmic knowledge is required, any user willing to have a somewhat manipulative conversation can plausibly attempt it. This changes the risk model for content moderation and safety teams, defenses tuned to catch unusual looking adversarial text, garbled suffixes or strange token sequences, will not catch an attack that reads as completely normal conversation, so filtering strategies built primarily around detecting anomalous input are likely insufficient on their own. The authors' own conclusion, that current defenses have a real gap here and more fundamental mitigations are needed for interactive systems, means organizations should treat persuasion style manipulation as an ongoing, unresolved risk category for any deployed conversational AI today, not a solved problem to check off.
explain_practitioner: The authors build a taxonomy of persuasion techniques grounded in established social science literature on influence and compliance, then use it to construct Persuasive Adversarial Prompts (PAP), natural, conversational prompts that reframe a harmful request using specific persuasion strategies rather than relying on adversarial suffixes, token level optimization, or unnatural looking text. Tested against Llama-2-7b-Chat, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 across ten trials per prompt, PAP achieves an attack success rate above 92 percent across all tested models and risk categories, which the authors report as exceeding the success rates of algorithm focused jailbreak methods evaluated for comparison. Because PAP prompts read as ordinary human conversation rather than adversarial looking text, they are also harder for keyword or perplexity based filters to catch than optimization based attacks, which tend to produce unnatural token sequences. The authors state directly that existing defenses show a significant gap against this persuasion based attack class, and argue the field needs more fundamental safety mitigations for models used in highly interactive, conversational settings, rather than defenses tuned mainly to catch algorithmically generated adversarial text.
